metadata.title: Matrices and Fake 3D
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: A matrix is a saved move, and it can flip a card

beats.narration_text: Matrices and Fake Three D. Learn what a matrix does to a point, how to combine moves, and how to flip a flat picture like a card.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Matrices have a reputation: advanced math, the part you skip. They are simpler than that. A matrix is a saved move, a small table of numbers that moves any point you give it.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A vector is a bundle of numbers, here a point's position. A matrix is a grid of numbers in rows and columns. A vertex is a corner point of a shape. A uniform is a value your game sets from outside. And a radian is Godot's angle unit: a full turn is tau, about six point two eight.

terms.meaning: a bundle of two to four numbers
a grid of numbers in rows and columns
a corner point of a shape
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one
Godot's angle unit; a full turn is tau, about 6.283

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: Watch a flat picture turn over like a card. No three-D model, no animation file. Every corner of the shape is multiplied by a small table of numbers. Learn that table, and you can spin, shrink, slide and flip anything you draw.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'A Table That Moves Points' (serif 40) top-left. Label under the window: 'scripted sweep'.

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: Take a point: five across, six down. Multiply it by a table of four numbers. Top row first: one times five plus three times six is twenty-three. Bottom row: two times five plus four times six is thirty-four.

shot.visual_intent: Left to right on the cream stage: a bracketed two-by-two table (1 3 over 2 4) labelled 'table', a bracketed column (5 over 6) labelled 'point', an equals sign and an empty bracketed result column. A terracotta ring outlines the table's top row (labelled 'row'); the small products '1 x 5' and '3 x 6' appear beneath and add up to '23', which lands in the first result slot. The ring drops to the bottom row: '2 x 5' and '4 x 6' add up to '34'. Last, a drawn arrow runs from the point column to the result column.

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: Look at the numbers in the code: one, two, then three, four. Godot reads each vec two as a column. So one, two stands upright on the left, and the table's top row is one, three.

On the right an empty bracketed two-by-two table. The first vec2 (1, 2) lifts out of the code and stands upright as the table's left column, labelled 'column'; the second (3, 4) becomes the right column. Then the top row is outlined and labelled 'row: 1, 3'.

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: Mix it up and nothing complains. Read the numbers as rows, and the answer is seventeen, thirty-nine. Put the point on the left of the table, and you get seventeen, thirty-nine again. Table first, point second.

Middle (grey, with a terracotta strike line): the numbers read as ROWS, so the table becomes 1 2 over 3 4 (the 2 and the 3 swap places) and the result is (17, 39); label 'rows'. Bottom (grey, with a strike line): the point written on the LEFT of the table, (5, 6) x table, result (17, 39); the code label 'p * table' beside it. At the end the top line is ringed and a label 'table first' lands.

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: Here is why columns make sense. The first column is where one step across lands. The second is where one step down lands. Five steps of the first and six of the second add up to twenty-three, thirty-four.

shot.visual_intent: A grid in Godot's screen directions (x to the right, y DOWN; small axis labels). The unit square with an 'across' arrow (solid) and a 'down' arrow (dashed). At the top right the table 1 3 over 2 4 with its first column outlined solid and its second dashed. The grid warps: the across arrow lands at (1, 2), the down arrow at (3, 4), the square becomes a parallelogram with corners (0,0), (1,2), (4,6), (3,4); tip labels '1, 2' and '3, 4'. Then the view zooms out and a staircase of five across-steps then six down-steps walks from the origin to a terracotta dot labelled '23, 34'.

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: The plainest table leaves both arrows where they started: one, zero, then zero, one. That is the identity matrix, and it moves nothing. In Godot, mat two of one gives exactly that table.

The four entries change to 1 0 over 0 1 and the grid relaxes back into the plain unit square while both arrows spring back onto (1, 0) and (0, 1). A label 'identity: moves nothing'. A small code card then shows mat2(1.0).

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: Stretch the arrows and the table scales. Two, zero, then zero, two lands each arrow twice as far out, so every point ends up twice as far from the middle.

beats.act: I · A Table That Moves Points
beats.narration_text: A shape is made of its corners. Multiply every corner by the same table and the whole shape follows. Four corners, one table: a move saved in four numbers.

beats.narration_text: Now something real. Godot calls the vertex function once per corner of a shape, and hands it the corner's position in pixels from the node's origin. On a centered sprite, that is the middle. Multiply it by the scale table, and the picture grows.

The card grows when the scale line is highlighted.

beats.narration_text: Turning is a table too. Turn by an angle, and the across arrow lands at cosine, sine. Those are how far across and how far down you get on a circle of radius one. The down arrow lands at minus sine, cosine.

At the right the table cos -sin over sin cos with its four live entries (0.71 -0.71 over 0.71 0.71), first column outlined solid and second dashed. A small label under the circle: 'across and down on a circle of radius one'.

beats.narration_text: Angles are in radians, so a full turn is about six point two eight, which Godot calls tau. Sweep the angle up to an eighth of tau and the picture turns clockwise, because on screen y points down.

beats.narration_text: Sliding is different. Whatever two by two table you pick, the point at zero, zero stays at zero, zero, because zero times anything is zero. A two by two table can scale and turn, but it cannot slide.

shot.visual_intent: The screen-direction grid with the origin pinned by a terracotta dot and a small pin drawn from lines. Three different two-by-two tables act in turn (a scale, a turn, a squash): the grid stretches, spins and squashes, but the origin dot never leaves its spot. At the end the whole grid tries to slide right (a dashed arrow) and snaps back; label '0, 0 stays 0, 0'.

shot.motion_claim: The grid stretches, spins and squashes around a dot that never moves; a slide is attempted and snaps back.

lecture.why: 'Cannot slide' is a limit; a pinned dot that survives three different warps shows the limit better than the sentence.

beats.narration_text: The fix is one extra number. Give the point a third number, always one, and use a three by three table. Put the slide in the last column: the top row now gives x plus the slide, and the bottom row keeps the one.

shot.visual_intent: A bracketed three-by-three table (1 0 100 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 1) with its last column outlined and labelled 'slide'; beside it a bracketed column (30 / 20 / 1) with its last slot ringed, labelled 'point, plus a one'; an equals sign and a result column. The ring walks down: the top row gives 1 x 30 + 0 x 20 + 100 x 1 = 130 (the 100 pairs with the one); the middle row gives 20; the bottom row gives 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, so the result column reads (130 / 20 / 1).

beats.narration_text: In the shader, put a one on the end of the corner's position, multiply, and keep the first two numbers. The slide sits in the last column, and the picture moves a hundred pixels to the right.

beats.narration_text: Three moves, three tables. Scale puts its numbers on the diagonal. Turn puts cosine and sine in the first two columns. Slide puts the offset in the last column. None of them bends an edge, so four moved corners are enough.

beats.narration_text: A slide alone is simpler as plain addition. Tables pay off when moves combine: a scale, a turn and a slide saved as one table. Then every corner needs one multiplication, not three.

beats.narration_text: To multiply tables, they must be the same size. Copy a two by two into the corner of a three by three, with zeros around it and a one in the bottom right. Godot does it for you: mat three of a mat two.

The two-by-two slides into its top left corner; zeros fill the rest of the grid in grey and a terracotta ring settles on the bottom right entry, which becomes 1: the table reads 0 -1 0 / 1 0 0 / 0 0 1. A small code card then shows mat3(turn).

beats.narration_text: Multiply two tables and you get one table that does both moves. The rule is the one you know: each entry is a row of the left table times a column of the right.

beats.narration_text: Which move happens first? The one nearest the point. Slide times turn, times point, turns first, then slides. Read it from the right, the way the point meets the tables.

props.command: Write a Godot canvas item shader that swings a sprite like a door. A float uniform called flip, from zero to one, is the fraction of a full turn around the vertical axis. A uniform called pivot, in pixels from the sprite's origin, is the hinge. Then point me to the lines that move the pivot.
output: Check: at flip zero, the sprite looks exactly as it did before the shader.
Check: with the pivot on the left edge, that edge stays put while the card swings.
